title: Naming what is wrong — Image Wiki
text:
Naming what is wrong
  A checklist for turning "something looks off" into a specific, defensible sentence about the image.

  
    Termvisual diagnostics
    Also calledimage critique, fault finding
    Not the same astaste, style, subject matter
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        1. Does all the light agree?2. Is anything floating?3. Do the surfaces behave like their materials?4. Does the space hold together?5. Does the blur follow the geometry?6. Does the image separate and settle?Keep defects and preferences apart
      
    
  

  "Something looks off about it" is a real perception and a useless report. You noticed a genuine inconsistency; the part of you that noticed just cannot talk. This page is a translation table.
Most defects are not matters of taste. They are things in the image that contradict each other. Your visual system has spent your whole life learning how light, surfaces and space behave, and it fires a quiet alarm when two parts of a picture imply two different physical worlds. Look deliberately and you can almost always find the contradiction.
Work through these in order. Stop when you find something concrete — you do not need to run the whole list.



Walker Evans, Bud Fields and his family at home, Hale County, Alabama, 1936. Library of Congress, public domain.
Worth running the checklist on a photograph that passes, so you know what agreement looks like. The window at the right edge is blown white, and the floorboards get steadily darker as they run away from it — one source, and the falloff proves where it is. Every bare foot and every chair leg has a small, tight, dark seam where it meets the floor: nobody is hovering. The floorboards and the wall boards converge consistently, and everyone's eye level sits at the same height, which is what tells you the camera was low, at about the height of a seated adult.
None of that is what the picture is about. It is the substrate that lets you believe the room exists.


1. Does all the light agree?
Shadows are the evidence. Highlights lie more easily. Pick two or three separate objects and check four things against each other:

Direction. Every shadow points away from the same place. See Light direction.
Softness. Shadow edges in one light are about equally crisp. Razor-sharp under one object and a soft gradient under another usually means an image assembled from parts. See Hard and soft light.
Colour. The lit sides should share a colour cast and the shadows should share theirs. A warmly lit subject standing in a scene lit by cold overcast is the most common composite tell there is. See The colour of the light.
Strength. If the sun is strong enough to blow out the wall, it is strong enough to put a dark shadow under the chin. Weak shadows with strong highlights do not belong together.




Marion Post Wolcott, Negro man entering movie theatre by the "colored" entrance, Belzoni, Mississippi, October 1939. Farm Security Administration, Library of Congress. Public domain.
Two unrelated shadows, one answer. The stairway's canopy throws a big wedge of dark across the brick, down and to the right of its own edge; the folding ladder standing against the white wall throws a smaller one in the same direction, at the same slant. Sun high and to our left, and only one of it. Both edges are hard lines you could trace with a pencil, which is the second agreement: one small source, so nothing in the frame is allowed a soft edge.
Then use the ladder for step 2. Its shadow does not touch it — the dark shape sits well to the right of the real ladder, and that gap measures how far the ladder stands off the wall. An object flush against a surface has its shadow welded to it; an offset shadow means air behind. Either can be right, but the offset and the distance have to agree.


2. Is anything floating?
Where two surfaces touch, light cannot get in, so the darkest part of a normal scene is the seam: under the shoe, where the chair leg meets the floor, in the crease of an elbow. This contact shadow is small, tight and dark.
Missing it, or replacing it with a soft grey blob at the wrong offset, makes objects hover. See The anatomy of a shadow.
3. Do the surfaces behave like their materials?

Metal reflects its surroundings, and tints what it reflects. See Metal and everything else.
Non-metals reflect the light's colour, not their own. A red highlight on a red object is a material error.
Shininess is never uniform. Real surfaces get more reflective at glancing angles, so the rim of a ball is shinier than its middle. An object equally glossy everywhere looks like a video game from 2005. See Roughness and Fresnel.
Wet, transparent and translucent things each have their own signature — a wet surface darkens and gains sharp reflections; skin and leaves glow slightly where light passes through the thin parts.




Willem Kalf, Still Life with a Silver Jug and a Porcelain Bowl, c. 1656. Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam. Public domain.
The silver jug has almost no colour of its own. Read its surface and you are reading the room: black patches where it reflects the dark niche, a pale streak up its left flank, and a broad warm gold wash across its belly picked up from the gilt cup and the fruit standing beside it. Cover the neighbours and most of the jug's tone has no source. That is the test for metal — its shading is a distorted picture of what surrounds it, not a smooth ramp from light to dark.
Now the lemon in front. Its sheen is a pale, near-white bloom lying on top of the yellow, not a more intense yellow: a non-metal returns the light's own colour and keeps its body colour underneath. The porcelain bowl does the same along its rim. And look where the jug's foot and the lemon meet the ledge — a dark, tight seam under each, which is step 2 passing.


4. Does the space hold together?

Straight lines that should converge, converge. Each set of real-world parallels — table edges, doorway, street — aims at one shared point. See Linear perspective.
Eye level is one height, and size follows distance: if you are looking down on the table you are looking down on the cup, and a person twice as far away is half as tall.
Depth clues should not fight. Something cannot both overlap an object and be behind it, and haze that softens the distance should get stronger with distance, not appear in patches. See Depth cues.




Eugène Atget, Rue Saint-Rustique, Montmartre, Paris, March 1922. Museum of Modern Art. Public domain.
Three checks on one street. The kerb, the gutter and the base of the right-hand wall all run to the same small area at the top of the slope: one set of parallel lines, one meeting point. The cobbles do the other half of the job — each stone is a known size, and they shrink and flatten steadily instead of in jumps, so distance and size stay in step the whole way up.
The subtlety is worth having. Because the street climbs, the point those lines meet at sits above your eye level rather than on the horizon. A slope does not break the rule, it moves the target — which is why "the lines meet somewhere sensible" is a stronger check than "the lines meet on the horizon".


5. Does the blur follow the geometry?
Real optical blur grows smoothly with distance from the focused plane, and everything at one distance is equally sharp. So:

A background uniformly blurred regardless of how far away each part is, is a blur filter, not a lens.
One side of an object sharp and the other soft, at the same distance, is wrong.
A crisp boundary between a sharp subject and a blurred background — especially one that follows the subject's outline — is a cut-out. See Depth of field.

6. Does the image separate and settle?
Now leave physics and ask whether the picture works as a picture.

Squint. Does the subject still exist, or does it dissolve into the background? See Value structure.
Is there one clear place for the eye to go, or several competing? See Visual hierarchy.
Anything merging with an edge, growing out of a head, or awkwardly cropped? See Gestalt grouping.


One tell is evidence, not proof
Real photographs contain every one of these anomalies sometimes. Studios use several lights of different sizes; gels make mismatched colour on purpose; tilt-shift lenses put the sharp plane somewhere strange; a genuine reflection can look impossible until you find the window causing it. Weigh how many independent things disagree, and how badly. One odd shadow is a curiosity. Three unrelated contradictions in one frame is a conclusion.

Keep defects and preferences apart
Two different sentences, and mixing them up wastes everyone's time:

"This is broken." The image contains a contradiction: two light directions, a floating object, impossible perspective. Not negotiable, not a matter of taste.
"This is not to my taste." Centred composition, muted palette, heavy grain, a face cropped at the forehead. All of these are deliberate choices somewhere, and none of them is a fault by itself.

When you are asked to judge an image, the first kind of sentence is worth far more than the second. If your only complaint is in the second category, say so plainly rather than dressing it up as a defect.

The fast pass

Two shadows — same direction, same softness, same colour?
Contact points — is anything floating?
Any metal or glass — does it reflect a plausible world?
Converging lines — do they agree on where they meet?
Blur — does it grow with distance, or was it painted on?
Squint — does the subject survive?

              Metal and everything else
              Metals have almost no colour of their own and show you the room instead; everything else gets its colour from underneath and reflects the light's own colour on top. This is the sharpest material test you can run on an image.
            
          
        
          
            
              Depth of field
              The band of distance that comes out looking sharp. Everything outside it blurs, and how that blur grows tells you whether a picture came out of a real camera.
